answer:
**Recommendation: don't add this month. Hold your current LEAPS and wait for evidence on Pellham.**

- **Pricing gives no reason to buy now.** Implied volatility is 27%, against a 2-year median of 26%. Skew is flat. The LEAPS are fairly priced, neither cheap nor expensive (n4). I didn't see actual premiums, strikes or expiries, so I couldn't check theta cost or compare prices to a model.
- **The headline demand view is positive, but it is out of date.** Planned 2027 utility capex is up 18% at Pellham Power and 12% at Norvane Utilities. Data-centre grid connection requests are expected to grow 9%, which is slower than 2026 (n2). n2 looked only at planned spending and connection requests, not at orders or backlogs.
- **Pellham's funding problem undercuts that demand view.** Pellham withdrew a C$2.4B equity offering after demand fell short. It is now cutting 2027 transformer orders by about 40% and deferring two substation programmes (n3). Pellham is 35% of VLTX's utility orders, and utilities are about 62% of all orders.
- **Norvane looks fundable.** It priced a C$1.1B bond comfortably, so its 12% increase looks achievable with debt. Norvane is 21% of utility orders. Bond spreads have widened 30bp to 165bp, so borrowing costs more. Two other utility share offerings were also cut back in size.
- **Concentration risk may not be in the price.** Pellham and Norvane together make up most of the utility demand. A 27% implied volatility may not fully price in a cut by the largest customer.

**Gaps:**
- The sources don't cover leverage, credit ratings, debt maturities or whether Pellham will retry its offering.
- The financing findings rest on three short documents.
- None of the sources is a VLTX price or earnings view.

**What would change the call:**
- Adding becomes reasonable if Pellham restores its orders or completes a financing.
- It would also be reasonable if implied volatility fell below its median, or if you can buy on a pullback.
